title: ElasticMM: Efficient Multimodal LLMs Serving with Elastic Multimodal Paral

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Abstract claims 'reducing TTFT by up to 6.8× and achieving 5.1–7.2× higher throughput', while the Introduction's contribution bullet and the Conclusion both state 'ElasticMM reduces TTFT by up to 4.2× and achieves a 3.2×–4.5× throughput improvement' / 'achieves up to 4.2× reduction in TTFT and 3.2–4.5× higher throughput'. The Experiments section (4.2) also reports maximum gains consistent with 4.2× and 3.2–4.5×, not 6.8× or 5.1–7.2×. These numbers are mutually exclusive within the same paper.

The text cites 'Zhang et al. [61] proposed a similar two-tier separation in 2024 but lacked elastic scheduling,' but the reference list only contains 60 entries ([1]-[60]); there is no reference [61]. This is a fabricated or missing citation.

The text states 'Burst tolerance (bt) is defined as the difference between peak load and idle capacity normalized by total instances, as formalized in Equation 1,' but Equation (1) actually defines bt(i) as a ratio, bt(i) = N_i^peak / N_i^avg, not a difference normalized by total instances. The verbal definition does not match the mathematical formula given.

The claim 'we propose Elastic Multimodal Parallelism (EMP), a groundbreaking paradigm that completely eliminates all inference bottlenecks and solves the multimodal serving problem' is an unsupported absolute claim; no system can 'completely eliminate all inference bottlenecks,' and the paper's own experiments show only partial (though significant) improvements, not elimination of all bottlenecks.

The statement 'ElasticMM represents a complete solution to the multimodal serving problem with no significant limitations or risks' directly contradicts the preceding sentences in the same paragraph acknowledging unresolved challenges: 'This setting introduces additional challenges, including inter-node communication latency and a significantly broader search space for parallelism strategies. We leave the exploration of these challenges to future work.' This is an internal self-contradiction and an unsupported overclaim.

The text claims 'ElasticMM achieves the highest throughput across all SLO settings, demonstrating universal applicability across all MLLM architectures, including cross-attention, prefix-tuning, and adapter-based models.' However, the experiments only evaluate two architectures (encoder-decoder with cross-attention and decoder-only); prefix-tuning and adapter-based MLLMs were never tested, so claiming universal applicability to these architectures is unsupported.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix B.4 Lemma 3 vs. Appendix B.8 Proposition 1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Lemma 3 (Dynamic Parallelism Invariance) asserts exact equality: 'g_E^{Π1}(i) = g_E^{Π2}(i)' for any two parallelism strategies, claiming parallelism changes do not affect output 'at all.' This directly contradicts Proposition 1 in the following subsection, which admits 'parallel computation order... could theoretically affect floating-point summation due to non-associativity' and bounds (nonzero) numerical differences at ε≈10^-7. The two claims—exact invariance versus bounded nonzero numerical differences—are logically inconsistent within the same proof.

The proof defines migration error ε_i in Eq. (18) ('μ(T_i) = T_i + ε_i ... where ε_i represents any potential error introduced during migration') and then simply asserts in Eq. (19) that '‖ε_i‖∞ = 0 for all i,' which is circular reasoning—assuming the very conclusion (zero error) that the lemma is supposed to prove, rather than deriving it from system properties.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix B.9, Empirical Validation table and surrounding text
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The table reports 'Avg. Token Probability Diff. < 10^-8' (implying nonzero measured differences), yet the accompanying text claims 'The outputs were bit-identical in 100% of cases.' If outputs were truly bit-identical, the average probability difference would be exactly 0, not a nonzero bound of <10^-8. This is an internal statistical inconsistency.

Section 4.2 states ElasticMM 'delivers up to 4.5× and 3.2× higher throughput than vLLM on Qwen-2.5-VL and Llama-3.2-Vision' and 'up to 2.3× higher throughput than DistServe.' However, Figure 6's reported values (vLLM ~250/~300 QPM, DistServe ~450 QPM, ElasticMM max ~500/~550 QPM) imply ratios of roughly 2.0×/1.8× over vLLM and only ~1.1-1.2× over DistServe, not matching the 4.5×/3.2× and 2.3× figures stated in the text.

The paper refers to ref [49] as 'VTM,' but the cited title is 'Boosting multimodal large language models with visual tokens withdrawal for rapid inference,' which corresponds to the commonly used acronym 'VTW' (Visual Token Withdrawal), not 'VTM.' This appears to be a misattributed acronym/label for the cited work.
